newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britain and China in last diplomatic wrangle on HK.
newsitem.headline: Britain and China in last diplomatic wrangle on HK.

text.p: Britain and China launched a final round on Wednesday of diplomatic horse-trading on Hong Kong before its handover to Beijing, amid a row over China-inspired plans to reshape the territory's election system.
The meeting of the Joint Liaison Group (JLG), headed by ambassadors from the two countries, faced a tricky question of the forum's own future, officials said.

Britain is keen to keep the JLG going to monitor China's compliance with the 1984 Sino-British handover treaty and other documents which promised Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy and the preservation of its capitalist way of life.
"The main area where a quarrel might erupt in this round is on the future of the JLG itself after the handover," said a Western diplomat well briefed on the talks.

"China clearly wants to play down the JLG's role, but Britain sees it as a forum where it can monitor and criticise if need be China's handling of Hong Kong after July 1. China sees Britain increasingly as an irrelevance," he said.
An official said the three-day session would also try to "cross the "t"s, dot the "i"s on the joint handover ceremony".
The extravaganza, to be attended by 4,000 VIPs including Chinese and British leaders, and billed as Asia's party of the century, is scheduled for midnight June 30.
Then, 156 years of colonial rule will end in a military pageant, a solemn flag raising ceremony and a sky full of fireworks.

A big political quarrel is raging between pro-China and pro-democracy forces in Hong Kong over future leader Tung Chee-hwa's plan, inspired by China, to reverse the liberal electoral reforms of departing Governor Chris Patten.
Patten and other critics say it is designed to hamper the popular Democratic Party from winning seats in 1998 elections.

After an avalanche of criticism for not consulting the public on the issue, Tung did a U-turn on Tuesday and agreed to accept comments from the community over the next two weeks before finalising the new election rules.
The JLG will also tackle "legal issues", which could lead to bickering over attempts by the future government to legislate through an appointed shadow legislature.
Other items up for discussion include the transfer of Hong Kong government assets and archives to the new government.
It will be the 40th round of JLG talks since they began in 1985 as a bargaining shop to elaborate on details of the handover, based on the 1984 handover treaty.
Over the years the talks have produced accords on areas such as the construction of a new airport, due to open next April.

It also produced a deal allowing China to send advance troops of the People's Liberation Army garrison into Hong Kong before the handover, another on the sell-off of former defence lands, and a government budget to straddle the handover.
But ideological disputes over human rights and democracy have dogged the JLG, with China's bloody 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy protests in Beijing hardening Britain's stance.
One analyst said the JLG had basically "prepared the ground to turn Hong Kong from a British colony into a Chinese colony".

The handover ceremony deal remained elusive until recently. And no agreement has been reached on vital issues such as the right of abode of Hong Kong people, or China's plans to reshape Hong Kong's political system to its own liking.

Rejecting fierce critcism from Britain and from Hong Kong democrats, China plans to dissolve the elected legislature and install a provisional lawmaking body on July 1, and to roll back the liberal civil rights and electoral laws.
